content: Warnings Hypersensitivity Before starting treatment with ceftriaxone, it is essential to thoroughly assess whether the patient has a history of hypersensitivity reactions to cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. Ceftriaxone should be used cautiously in patients with a known sensitivity to penicillin. Antibiotics, including ceftriaxone, should be administered with caution in patients who have demonstrated any form of allergy, particularly to medications. Severe acute hypersensitivity reactions, such as anaphylaxis, may occur and could require immediate administration of subcutaneous epinephrine and other emergency interventions. Interaction with Calcium-Containing Products Ceftriaxone should not be reconstituted or diluted with calcium-containing solutions, such as Ringer’s solution or Hartmann’s solution, as this can lead to the formation of precipitates. Precipitation of ceftriaxone-calcium can also occur when ceftriaxone is mixed with calcium-containing solutions in the same intravenous (IV) line. Ceftriaxone must not be administered simultaneously with calcium-containing IV solutions, including continuous infusions like parenteral nutrition, via a Y-site. However, in patients other than neonates, ceftriaxone and calcium-containing solutions may be given sequentially if the infusion lines are thoroughly flushed with a compatible fluid between administrations. Neonates are at an increased risk of ceftriaxone-calcium precipitation, as demonstrated in in vitro studies using adult and neonatal plasma from umbilical cord blood. Clostridium difficile-Associated Diarrhea (CDAD) Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including ceftriaxone. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibiotic treatment disrupts the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and could require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea after antibiotic use, even if it occurs up to two months after treatment. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotics not directed against C. difficile may be necessary. Management should include appropriate fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation if clinically indicated. Hemolytic Anemia Immune-mediated hemolytic anemia has been observed in patients receiving cephalosporins, including ceftriaxone. Severe cases, including fatalities, have been reported in both adults and children during treatment. If a patient develops anemia while on ceftriaxone, the possibility of cephalosporin-associated hemolytic anemia should be considered, and ceftriaxone should be discontinued until the cause is determined. Precautions General Ceftriaxone should only be prescribed when there is a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a clear prophylactic indication. Unnecessary use increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. While transient elevations in blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine have been observed, the nephrotoxic potential of ceftriaxone at recommended doses is similar to other cephalosporins. Ceftriaxone is excreted through both biliary and renal pathways, and dosage adjustments are generally not required in patients with renal failure. However, in patients with both hepatic dysfunction and significant renal disease, the daily dose should not exceed 2 grams, and caution is advised. Prolonged use of ceftriaxone may lead to overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, necessitating careful monitoring. Patients with a history of gastrointestinal disease, particularly colitis, should be treated with caution. Sonographic abnormalities in the gallbladder, such as sludge or shadowing resembling gallstones, have been reported in patients treated with ceftriaxone. These findings are typically transient and reversible upon discontinuation of the drug. If symptoms of gallbladder disease occur, ceftriaxone should be stopped, and conservative management should be initiated. Rare cases of pancreatitis, potentially secondary to biliary obstruction, have also been reported, particularly in patients with risk factors for biliary stasis or sludge. Information for Patients Patients should be informed that ceftriaxone is only effective against bacterial infections and does not treat viral infections, such as the common cold. They should be advised to complete the full course of therapy as prescribed, even if they feel better early in the treatment. Skipping doses or not completing the therapy may reduce the effectiveness of the treatment and increase the risk of developing antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Patients should also be made aware that diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics, which usually resolves after discontinuation. However, if they develop watery or bloody stools, with or without stomach cramps and fever, even up to two months after completing the antibiotic, they should contact their physician immediately. Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, and Impairment of Fertility No carcinogenicity studies have been conducted with ceftriaxone due to the limited duration of treatment and the nature of the drug class. Genetic toxicology tests, including the Ames test, micronucleus test, and chromosomal aberration test in human lymphocytes, showed no evidence of mutagenic potential. In animal studies, ceftriaxone did not impair fertility when administered intravenously to rats at doses up to 20 times the recommended human dose. Pregnancy Ceftriaxone is classified as Pregnancy Category B. Animal studies in mice and rats at doses up to 20 times the human dose showed no evidence of embryotoxicity, fetotoxicity, or teratogenicity. Similarly, no adverse effects were observed in primates at doses approximately three times the human dose. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, so ceftriaxone should only be used during pregnancy if clearly necessary. Nursing Mothers Ceftriaxone is excreted in low concentrations in human breast milk. Caution should be exercised when administering ceftriaxone to nursing mothers. Pediatric Use Ceftriaxone has been shown to be safe and effective in neonates, infants, and pediatric patients at the recommended dosages. However, it should not be administered to hyperbilirubinemic neonates, particularly premature infants, as it may displace bilirubin from serum albumin, increasing the risk of bilirubin encephalopathy. Geriatric Use In clinical studies, 32% of participants were aged 60 or older. No significant differences in safety or efficacy were observed between older and younger patients. Pharmacokinetics of ceftriaxone are minimally altered in elderly patients, and dosage adjustments are not required for doses up to 2 grams per day. However, some elderly individuals may exhibit greater sensitivity to the drug.
